title: The Crown from the Gutter: How Germany's 1848 Revolution Won Everything and Lost It All
description:
In March 1848, Berliners tore up their streets, built barricades, and forced the King of Prussia to bow before their dead. Within weeks, Metternich had fled Vienna and Germany's first freely elected parliament was meeting in Frankfurt's St Paul's Church. A year later, that parliament offered the king the crown of a united, constitutional Germany. He refused it. By the summer of 1849, the last revolutionaries were surrendering at the fortress of Rastatt.

This video follows the people at the centre of it: Friedrich Wilhelm IV, the romantic king who despised a crown offered by the people; Heinrich von Gagern, the parliament's president, whose own brother died fighting the radicals; Robert Blum, the Cologne pauper turned deputy who was shot in Vienna; Friedrich Hecker, the republican who ended up a colonel in the American Civil War; and Carl Schurz, who escaped Rastatt through a sewer and became a US senator. Why did the revolution fail, and why does modern Germany still fly its colours?

scenes.narration: Berlin. The night of the eighteenth of March, 1848. Church bells ring the alarm across the city. Paving stones are torn up and piled into walls. Behind them wait students, craftsmen and apprentices, facing the army of their own king. By morning, hundreds lie dead. And the king will give in. So why did a revolution that won almost everywhere that spring lose everything a year later?

scenes.narration: This is the story of Germany's first attempt to build a free, united nation from below, and of a crown that nobody wanted to wear.

visuals.file: File:Image Germania (painting).jpg
visuals.caption: Germania, the banner painting that hung in St Paul's Church, Frankfurt, 1848

scenes.narration: In 1848 there was no Germany. There was a loose German Confederation of nearly forty states, from mighty Austria and Prussia down to tiny principalities. Princes ruled by the grace of God. Newspapers were censored, and the architect of that order was Austria's chancellor, Prince Metternich. And people were hungry: potato blight and failed harvests had sent food prices soaring.

visuals.file: File:Metternich by Lawrence.jpeg
visuals.caption: Prince Klemens von Metternich, Austrian chancellor

visuals.file: File:Zug auf das Schloss Hambach 1832 Deutschland.png
visuals.caption: Liberals march to Hambach Castle under black-red-gold, 1832

scenes.narration: Then, in late February, Paris rose. In three days of street fighting the French king was driven from his throne. On the thirteenth of March, students marched in Vienna. Troops fired. That same day, Metternich resigned, and soon the man who had dominated Europe for over thirty years was an exile in England.

visuals.file: File:Henri Félix Philippoteaux - Lamartine repoussant le drapeau rouge à l'Hôtel de Ville, le 25 février 1848 - P258 - Musée Carnavalet.jpg
visuals.caption: Paris, 25 February 1848: Lamartine before the Hôtel de Ville

visuals.file: File:BACH(1898) p289 Barricade auf dem Stefansplatz am 26.05.1848.jpg
visuals.caption: Barricade on Stephansplatz, Vienna, May 1848

scenes.narration: In Berlin, King Friedrich Wilhelm the Fourth hesitated. A romantic who believed he ruled by divine right, he loathed the idea of a written constitution. On the eighteenth of March a crowd filled the square before his palace. Two shots rang out, probably by accident. Within hours the city was a fortress of barricades, by one count more than nine hundred. After a night of fighting, the king blinked. He promised reforms and pulled his troops out of the city.

visuals.file: File:1846 Krueger Friedrich Wilhelm IV anagoria.JPG
visuals.caption: King Friedrich Wilhelm IV of Prussia, by Franz Krüger, 1846

visuals.file: File:Barrikade in der Breiten Straße.jpg
visuals.caption: Barricade on Breite Straße, Berlin, March 1848

visuals.file: File:1848 Barrikadenkampf vor dem köllnischen Rathause zu Berlin.jpg
visuals.caption: Fighting at the Cölln town hall, Berlin, 18–19 March 1848

scenes.narration: The next afternoon, the people carried their dead to the palace, bodies uncovered, wounds on display. They called for the king. When he appeared, the crowd shouted: hats off! And the King of Prussia bared his head before the men his soldiers had killed. Two days later he rode through Berlin wearing a black, red and gold armband, the colours of German unity. It looked like total victory.

visuals.file: File:Aufbahrung der Märzgefallenen (1848) Adolf Friedrich Erdmann von Menzel (Hamburger Kunsthalle).jpg
visuals.caption: Adolph Menzel, The Laying Out of the March Dead, 1848

visuals.file: File:Leichenbegängniss der in den Märztagen Gefallenen am 22. März.png
visuals.caption: Funeral of the March dead, Berlin, 22 March 1848

visuals.file: File:Franz Krüger - Porträt des Königs Friedrich Wilhelm IV. von Preußen.jpg
visuals.caption: Friedrich Wilhelm IV

scenes.narration: But not everyone wanted to negotiate with kings. In Baden, a fiery lawyer named Friedrich Hecker wanted a republic, now. In April he called the people to arms. He hoped for tens of thousands. A few thousand came. Near the village of Kandern, government troops met his volunteers. Their commander, General Friedrich von Gagern, tried to talk them into surrender, and was shot dead. Hecker fled to Switzerland. And the dead general's younger brother was about to lead Germany's first parliament.

visuals.file: File:Illustrirte Chronik Friedrich Hecker 1848.jpg
visuals.caption: Friedrich Hecker, 1848

visuals.file: File:"Morgen brechen wir auf" - Friedrich Hecker in Konstanz.jpg
visuals.caption: Modern mural of Hecker and his volunteers, Konstanz

visuals.file: File:"Tod des Generals Friedrich Freiherrn von Gagern, bei Kandern am 20. April (1848)." - LABW - Generallandesarchiv Karlsruhe J-G G 1.jpg
visuals.query: Tod des Generals von Gagern Kandern 1848
visuals.caption: Death of General Friedrich von Gagern near Kandern, 20 April 1848

scenes.narration: On the eighteenth of May, 1848, the first freely elected parliament for all of Germany filed into St Paul's Church in Frankfurt. Above them hung a painting of Germania, sword in hand. They chose Heinrich von Gagern as their president. So many lawyers and scholars sat in its benches that people mocked it as the professors' parliament. Now they had to write a constitution for a country that did not yet exist.

visuals.file: File:Paulskirche einzugparlamentarierer1848.jpg
visuals.caption: Deputies process into St Paul's Church, Frankfurt, May 1848

visuals.file: File:Zeitgenössige Lithografie der Nationalversammlung in der Paulskirche.jpg
visuals.caption: The National Assembly in session, St Paul's Church, 1848

visuals.file: File:Eduard von Heuss - Heinrich von Gagern, 1848.jpg
visuals.caption: Heinrich von Gagern, President of the National Assembly

scenes.narration: And they argued. Should Germany include Austria, and with it an empire of Czechs, Hungarians and Italians? Or should it be a smaller Germany, led by Prussia? While the speeches went on for months, the parliament had no army, no tax collectors, no police of its own. The kings still had all three. And in the autumn, they began to use them.

visuals.file: File:Frankfurt Am Main-Jakob Fuerchtegott Dielmann-FFMADIUSAAUNZ-021-Das Innere der Paulskirche als Parlamentshaus.jpg
visuals.caption: Inside St Paul's Church as a parliament, after Jakob Fürchtegott Dielmann

visuals.subtext: With Austria, or without it and led by Prussia

visuals.file: File:Frankfurt Nationalversammlung 1848.jpg
visuals.caption: The Frankfurt National Assembly, 1848

scenes.narration: Robert Blum was the voice of the left in Frankfurt. Born poor in Cologne, he had worked his way up from theatre servant to politician. In October 1848, Vienna rose again, and Blum went there with a delegation from Frankfurt. He joined the defenders. The imperial army stormed the city. Blum was arrested and claimed immunity as a member of the national parliament. It made no difference. Early on the ninth of November, he was shot by firing squad.

visuals.file: File:Portrait of Robert Blum by August Hunger.jpg
visuals.caption: Robert Blum, deputy for Leipzig

visuals.file: File:Kaiserliche Truppen vor den Stadtmauern Wiens 1848.jpg
visuals.caption: Imperial troops under Windischgrätz outside Vienna, October 1848

visuals.file: File:BACH(1898) p751 Sturmangriff auf eine Barricade in der Leopoldstadt, Oktober 1848.jpg
visuals.caption: Troops storm a barricade in Leopoldstadt, Vienna, October 1848

visuals.file: File:1848 Steffeck Robert Blums Ende anagoria.JPG
visuals.caption: Carl Steffeck, The End of Robert Blum, 1848

scenes.narration: His reported last words: I die for German freedom, for which I have fought. The next day, Prussian troops marched back into Berlin. The counter-revolution had begun.

visuals.text: I die for German freedom, for which I have fought. May the Fatherland remember me.
visuals.subtext: Robert Blum, reported last words, Vienna, 9 November 1848

visuals.file: File:RB-Hinrichtung.jpeg
visuals.caption: The execution of Robert Blum, Brigittenau, 9 November 1848

scenes.narration: Yet Frankfurt kept working. In December it passed the Basic Rights of the German People: equality before the law, freedom of the press, of faith, of assembly, and the abolition of the death penalty in most cases. By March 1849 the constitution was done, with a hereditary emperor at its head. On the twenty-eighth of March, the parliament elected Friedrich Wilhelm the Fourth Emperor of the Germans. But the king had already made up his mind.

visuals.file: File:Heinrich von Gagern 1848.jpg
visuals.caption: Heinrich von Gagern, 1848

visuals.file: File:Eduard von Simson by Fritz Paulsen.jpg
visuals.caption: Eduard Simson, president of the assembly in 1849

visuals.subtext: Friedrich Wilhelm IV elected Emperor of the Germans: 290 votes, 248 abstentions

scenes.narration: Months earlier, in a private letter, he had called such a crown an imaginary hoop baked from mud and clay, reeking of revolution. On the third of April, 1849, Eduard Simson led the parliament's delegation into the royal palace in Berlin. The king would not accept. Within weeks the refusal was final. Twenty-eight smaller governments had accepted the constitution. Prussia and Austria did not. The great work of Frankfurt was dead on arrival.

visuals.text: Such an imaginary hoop, baked from mud and clay: should a legitimate king by the grace of God, and the King of Prussia at that, let himself be given it?
visuals.subtext: Friedrich Wilhelm IV, letter to Christian von Bunsen, 13 December 1848

visuals.file: File:Blos 527 Kaiserdeputation.jpg
visuals.caption: The imperial deputation before Friedrich Wilhelm IV, Berlin, 3 April 1849

visuals.file: File:Friedrich Wilhelm IV von preussen 1847.jpg
visuals.caption: Friedrich Wilhelm IV, c. 1847

scenes.narration: So the people tried to force it through. In May 1849, Dresden rose, with the composer Richard Wagner among the rebels. Saxon and Prussian troops crushed it within a week. In Baden, the soldiers of the fortress of Rastatt mutinied, and the Grand Duke fled his own country. What was left of the parliament retreated to Stuttgart. On the eighteenth of June, soldiers broke it up.

visuals.file: File:Gefechtsplan von Dresden 1849.jpg
visuals.caption: Battle plan of the Dresden May Uprising, 1849

visuals.file: File:Ausbruch des Aufstands in Rastatt 13 Mai 1849.jpg
visuals.caption: Uprising in Rastatt, May 1849

visuals.file: File:Württembergisches Militär im Einsatz gegen das Rumpfparlament 1849.jpg
visuals.caption: Württemberg troops disperse the rump parliament, Stuttgart, 18 June 1849

scenes.narration: Against Baden marched a Prussian army led by the king's brother, Prince Wilhelm. The rebels fell back into Rastatt. For three weeks the fortress held. On the twenty-third of July, 1849, it surrendered. Courts-martial followed, and twenty-seven men were executed in Baden. Inside Rastatt was a twenty-year-old student named Carl Schurz. He knew what awaited him. So he crawled out through an unguarded sewer and escaped across the Rhine into France.

visuals.file: File:Preußisches Lager bei Rauental.jpg
visuals.caption: Prussian camp at Rauental during the siege of Rastatt, 1849

visuals.file: File:Entwaffnung der Insurgentenbesatzung von Rastatt.jpg
visuals.caption: The rebel garrison of Rastatt is disarmed, July 1849

visuals.file: File:Gefangene Freischärler in einer Rastatter Kasematte.png
visuals.caption: Captured volunteers in a Rastatt casemate

scenes.narration: Schurz was not alone. Tens of thousands left Baden in the years that followed, driven by poverty as much as politics. Many went to America. They were called the Forty-Eighters. Friedrich Hecker became a farmer in Illinois and a colonel in the Union army. Carl Schurz became a Union general, a senator from Missouri, and Secretary of the Interior.

visuals.file: File:1849.Badensche Gefangene.jpg
visuals.caption: Prussian soldiers lead away prisoners in Baden, 1849

visuals.file: File:Carl Schurz 1879.jpg
visuals.caption: Carl Schurz, US Secretary of the Interior, 1879

visuals.file: File:Carl Schurz playing the piano for President Hayes and his family.jpg
visuals.caption: Carl Schurz at the piano for President Hayes and his family

scenes.narration: So why did it fail? The revolution won the streets in spring, then handed power back to the princes and asked them to share it. Liberals feared the radicals more than the kings. And when it came to the crown, the parliament needed the one man who despised it. Germany would be united in 1871, but by Prussian armies, not by a parliament. Its first emperor was the same Prince Wilhelm who had crushed Rastatt.

visuals.file: File:Tote Freischärler vor Rastatt.jpg
visuals.caption: Dead volunteers outside Rastatt, 1849

visuals.file: File:Weisenbach am 24. Juni 1849.jpg
visuals.caption: Fighting at Weisenbach, Baden, 24 June 1849

visuals.file: File:008241-Inv---WGM-Katalog-56---Rastatt-Festung-1857 web.jpg
visuals.caption: The fortress of Rastatt, 1857

scenes.narration: Yet the story does not end there. In 1919, the Weimar Republic made black, red and gold the national flag and borrowed from Frankfurt's basic rights. In 1949, the authors of West Germany's Basic Law quoted the Paulskirche constitution as they wrote. Its Article 22 says simply: the federal flag is black, red and gold. The men of 1848 lost every battle. But the country they imagined is the one Germany became.
